# Anatomy of a Quarto file {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Three kinds of content

A `.qmd` file is plain text, made of just three ingredients:

::: {.incremental}
- A [YAML header]{.highlight-peach}: the settings for the whole document
- [Prose]{.highlight-peach}: ordinary text written in Markdown
- [Code]{.highlight-peach}: chunks of R that run and produce output
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
You have used all three since Module 1. Today we look at each one more closely.
:::

## How they fit together

````` {.markdown}
---
title: "My report"
format: html
---

## Introduction

Some **prose** written in Markdown.

```{{r}}
1 + 1
```
`````

. . .

Header at the top, then prose and code chunks in any order.

# The YAML header {background-color="#4C326A"}

## What is YAML?

[YAML]{.highlight-peach} is a small language for settings. In Quarto it holds the document metadata: title, author, output format, and more.

. . .

It sits at the very top of the file, [delimited by three dashes]{.highlight-peach} above and below:

``` {.yaml}
---
title: "My report"
format: html
---
```

## The two rules of syntax

YAML is fussy about two things:

::: {.incremental}
- Write `key: value`, always with a [space after the colon]{.highlight-peach}
- Show nesting with [indentation]{.highlight-peach}, using two spaces, never tabs
:::

. . .

``` {.yaml}
format:
  html:
    toc: true
```

. . .

::: {.task}
`format:html` (no space) or a stray tab will break the render. When YAML misbehaves, check colons and indentation first.
:::

## Important YAML options

``` {.yaml}
---
title: "Penguin report"
subtitle: "A first analysis"
author: "Your Name"
date: "2026-07-02"
format: html
---
```

. . .

These set the visible front matter: what the reader sees at the top of the document.

## Controlling the output

``` {.yaml}
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
    code-fold: true
    theme: cosmo
---
```

::: {.incremental}
- `toc`: add a table of contents
- `number-sections`: number the headings
- `code-fold`: hide code behind a clickable toggle
- `theme`: pick a visual style
:::

## Execution options

You can also set defaults for [every code chunk]{.highlight-peach} in one place:

``` {.yaml}
execute:
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---
```

::: {.incremental}
- `echo`: show the code, not just its output
- `warning` and `message`: hide R's chatter from the report
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
A chunk option set on an individual chunk overrides the document default.
:::

## Common options: a reference

The header can hold far more than a title. These are the options you will reach for most, grouped by what they affect.

. . .

::: {.task}
Every option below goes in the YAML header. Format-specific ones sit nested under `format:`.
:::

## Document metadata

The front matter the reader sees, all set at the [top level]{.highlight-peach}:

| Option | What it sets |
|--------|--------------|
| `title` | The document title |
| `subtitle` | A secondary line under the title |
| `author` | Who wrote it |
| `date` | The date shown on the document |
| `abstract` | A short summary of the work |

. . .

::: {.task}
`date: today` fills in the render date for you, so it is never stale.
:::

## Contents and navigation

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `toc` | Add a table of contents |
| `toc-depth` | Lowest heading level to include, e.g. `2`, `3` |
| `number-sections` | Number the headings |
| `anchor-sections` | Show a link anchor when hovering a heading |

## Style and appearance

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `theme` | A Bootswatch theme: `cosmo`, `darkly`, `solar` |
| `css` | A CSS or SCSS file to style the document |
| `highlight-style` | Syntax highlighting theme: `arrow`, `kate`, `zenburn` |
| `mainfont`, `monofont` | Font family for text and for code |

## Code display

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `echo` | Show the code, not only its output |
| `code-fold` | Let readers toggle the code open and closed |
| `code-tools` | A menu to hide, show, or download the code |
| `code-overflow` | Wide code: `scroll` or `wrap` |

## Figures

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `fig-align` | Alignment: `default`, `left`, `right`, `center` |
| `fig-width`, `fig-height` | Default figure size, in inches |
| `fig-format` | Figure format: `retina`, `png`, `svg`, `pdf` |

. . .

::: {.task}
The full list of options, by format, lives at [quarto.org/docs/reference](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/).
:::

# Rendering {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Turning source into output

A `.qmd` is just source text. [Rendering]{.highlight-peach} runs the code and produces the finished document.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- In RStudio: the [Render]{.highlight-peach} button, or `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K`
- From the terminal: `quarto render report.qmd`
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
`quarto preview` renders and opens a live preview that refreshes every time you save.
:::

# Text formatting {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Markdown is the prose layer

Between chunks you write in [Markdown]{.highlight-peach}: a few plain-text marks that Quarto turns into formatted output.

. . .

You write `**bold**`, you get **bold**. The source stays readable.

## The everyday marks

| You write | You get |
|-----------|---------|
| `*italic*` | *italic* |
| `**bold**` | **bold** |
| `` `code` `` | `code` |
| `[link](url)` | a hyperlink |
| `# Heading` | a section heading |

. . .

::: {.task}
The number of `#` sets the heading level: `#` is a top-level section, `##` a subsection.
:::

## Lists

Bullet lists start each line with a dash:

``` {.markdown}
- first item
- second item
  - a nested item
```

. . .

Numbered lists use `1.`, `2.`, and so on. A blank line separates a list from the paragraph around it.

## Images and equations

Insert an image with an exclamation mark:

``` {.markdown}
![A caption](figures/plot.png)
```

. . .

Write mathematics in LaTeX, between dollar signs:

``` {.markdown}
The mean is $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i$.
```

. . .

renders as: the mean is $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i$.

## Code inside prose

Weave a computed value straight into a sentence with [inline code]{.highlight-peach}: a backtick, the letter `r`, then an expression.

``` {.markdown}
The dataset has `r knitr::inline_expr('nrow(penguins)')` rows.
```

. . .

On render it becomes: "The dataset has 344 rows."

. . .

::: {.task}
Numbers written this way update themselves on every render, so your prose never falls out of sync with your data.
:::

## Callout blocks

Quarto offers built-in callout boxes for notes and comments:

```` {.markdown}
::: {.callout-note}
Penguin data is from the `palmerpenguins` package.
:::
````

. . .

The type sets the colour and icon:

::: {.callout-note}
`.callout-note`: general information
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
`.callout-tip`: a helpful suggestion
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
`.callout-warning`: something to watch out for
:::

# Figures and tables {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Figures from code

Chunk options, the lines starting with `#|`, control how a plot appears:

```` {.markdown}
```{{r}}
#| label: fig-mass
#| fig-cap: "Body mass by species"
#| out-width: "80%"

ggplot(penguins, aes(species, body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```
````

. . .

`fig-cap` adds a caption, `out-width` sets the display size.

## Captions and cross-references

Give a chunk a `label` starting with `fig-`, then [refer to it]{.highlight-peach} by that label anywhere in the text:

``` {.markdown}
Species differ clearly in @fig-mass.
```

. . .

Quarto numbers the figure and inserts a link, exactly like the cross-references covered earlier in the course.

. . .

::: {.task}
Tables work the same way: a `tbl-` label with `#| tbl-cap:`, plus a table function such as `knitr::kable()` that you have already used, gives a captioned, referenceable table.
:::

# Citations and references {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Three words that get confused

::: {.incremental}
- A [citation]{.highlight-peach}: a pointer to a source in your text. Whenever you quote, paraphrase, or summarize someone else's idea, an in-text citation follows
- A [reference]{.highlight-peach}: the detailed description of that source, with author, title, year, publisher, DOI
- The [bibliography]{.highlight-peach}: the list of references at the end, usually alphabetical by author
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
You cite a source in the prose, its reference holds the details, and the bibliography gathers them all into one list.
:::

## Where references are stored

The reference details live in a separate file, usually [BibTeX]{.highlight-peach} (`.bib`). Each entry has a [citation key]{.highlight-peach}:

``` {.bibtex}
@book{wickham2023,
  title     = {R for Data Science},
  author    = {Wickham, Hadley and others},
  year      = {2023},
  publisher = {O'Reilly}
}
```

. . .

Here the key is `wickham2023`. That is how you refer to this entry.

## How a citation flows

You point Quarto at the file in the YAML:

``` {.yaml}
bibliography: references.bib
```

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- You write `[@wickham2023]` in the text
- Quarto inserts the citation marker there
- It automatically builds the matching reference at the end, i.e., only items that are cited appear in the reference list.
:::

. . .

To list works you did not cite or the entire `.bib` file, use the `nocite:` option in the YAML:

``` {.yaml}
nocite: |
  @wickham2023, @tidy2014
```
``` {.yaml}
nocite: |
  @*
```

# Scholarly articles {background-color="#4C326A"}

## Quarto for academic writing

Quarto can render a full [scholarly article]{.highlight-peach}: title, authors, affiliations, abstract, and a formatted reference list, all from one `.qmd`.

. . .

The structure is driven entirely by the YAML header.

## The article header

``` {.yaml}
---
title: "Penguins of the Palmer Archipelago"
author:
  - name: "Jane Doe"
    affiliation: "University of Somewhere"
    email: "jane.doe@example.edu"
abstract: |
  We examine body size across three penguin
  species and find clear differences by island.
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
format: pdf
---
```

## Reading the header

::: {.incremental}
- `author`, `affiliation`, `email`: who wrote it and where
- `abstract`: a short summary, indented under the `|` block
- `bibliography`: the `.bib` file of references
- `csl`: the [citation style]{.highlight-peach} that sets the formatting
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
The `|` after `abstract:` lets you write a multi-line value that keeps its line breaks.
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
Rendering to PDF needs a LaTeX engine. Install it once with `quarto install tinytex`.
:::

## Adding citations

Cite at the [end of a sentence]{.highlight-peach} with the key in square brackets:

``` {.markdown}
Tidy data has one row per observation [@wickham2014].
```

. . .

renders as: Tidy data has one row per observation (Wickham 2014).

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- `[@key]`: a parenthetical citation, in brackets
- `@key`: an in-text citation, "Wickham (2014) showed..."
- `[@key1; @key2]`: cite several works at once
:::

## Citations as numbers

By default, citations show author and year. To show them as [numbers]{.highlight-peach} instead, choose a numeric [CSL style]{.highlight-peach}:

``` {.yaml}
csl: ieee.csl
---
```

. . .

Now `[@wickham2014]` renders as `[1]`, and the references are listed in citation order.

. . .

::: {.task}
The CSL file alone controls the look. You change the style by swapping the file, never by editing your citations.
:::

# Publishing to GitHub Pages {background-color="#4C326A"}

## What is GitHub Pages?

[GitHub Pages]{.highlight-peach} is a free service that serves a website straight from a GitHub repository. It hosts [static pages]{.highlight-peach}: plain HTML, exactly what Quarto renders.

. . .

::: {.task}
Render your `.qmd` to HTML, push it to GitHub, and it is live on the web.
:::

## Two requirements

::: {.incremental}
- The repository must be [public]{.highlight-peach} (on a free account)
- The home page must be named [`index.html`]{.highlight-peach}
:::

. . .

GitHub looks for `index.html` as the entry point, the same way a website's front door is always `index`.

## The usual setup

A common layout renders the site into a `docs/` folder:

``` {.plain}
.
└── docs
    ├── index.qmd
    ├── references.bib
    └── index.html
```

. . .

In the repository settings, point Pages at the `docs/` folder on the main branch.

## Going live

::: {.incremental}
- Render `index.qmd` so `index.html` appears
- Commit and push to GitHub
- Enable Pages in the repository settings
- Visit `https://organization.github.io/repo`
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
After the first push, every later push that changes the HTML updates the live site automatically.
:::

## A single shareable file

No public repo? Bundle everything into [one self-contained HTML]{.highlight-peach} file:

``` {.yaml}
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---
```

. . .

Images, styles, and scripts are folded into the one `.html`, so you can email it or hand it over and it just works.

# Slides with Quarto {background-color="#4C326A"}

## reveal.js

Quarto builds slides from the same Markdown you already know. The HTML slide format is [reveal.js]{.highlight-peach}: set it in the YAML.

``` {.yaml}
---
title: "My talk"
format: revealjs
---
```

. . .

::: {.task}
These very slides are a `revealjs` Quarto document.
:::

## Headings make slides

The structure is simple:

::: {.incremental}
- `#` starts a new [section]{.highlight-peach}, a divider slide
- `##` starts a new [content]{.highlight-peach} slide
- Everything under a heading is that slide's content
:::

. . .

``` {.markdown}
## First slide

Some content here.

## Second slide

More content.
```

## Building content gradually

To reveal a slide in steps, put a line containing only `. . .` between the parts. Everything below it stays [hidden until the next click]{.highlight-peach}.

. . .

An incremental list reveals one bullet per click:

``` {.markdown}
::: {.incremental}
- appears first
- then this one
- then this one
:::
```

## Code and output on slides

Code chunks work exactly as in any Quarto document. You write:

```` {.markdown}
```{{r}}
1 + 1
```
````

. . .

and on the rendered slide you get both the code and its result:

```{r}
#| label: demo
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

1 + 1
```

## Presenting

::: {.incremental}
- Arrow keys move between slides
- `F` goes full screen, `Esc` shows an overview
- `S` opens speaker notes
- `?` lists every shortcut
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
The rendered slides are a single HTML file: publish them to GitHub Pages just like any other page.
:::

# What else can Quarto build? {background-color="#4C326A"}

## One source, many outputs

The same Markdown and code render into far more than a single report:

::: {.incremental}
- [Documents]{.highlight-peach}: HTML, PDF, Word
- [Presentations]{.highlight-peach}: reveal.js, PowerPoint, Beamer (PDF)
- [Websites]{.highlight-peach}: like [this course's site](https://ds4owd-002.github.io/website/)
- [Books]{.highlight-peach}: like [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/)
- [Dashboards]{.highlight-peach}: interactive panels, see the [gallery](https://quarto.org/docs/gallery/#dashboards)
- [Manuscripts]{.highlight-peach}: reproducible articles, as [HTML](https://jperkel.github.io/computed_quarto_manuscript/) or as PDF.
:::

. . .

::: {.task}
You can also use custom typst formats as templates: <https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html>
:::
